title: Segmented sub-wordline refresh restores only weak-cell segments
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation (contradiction: refresh often for the tail vs rarely for the bulk): reuse existing sub-wordline-driver boundaries so each 8 Kb row is 16 independently fired segments; a fuse-loaded 2-bit retention tag per segment lets the refresh engine fire only segments holding sub-256 ms cells at 64 ms while the rest refresh at 1 s.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: ~85-90% fewer segment restores, ~60% less refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth loss recovered at 32-64 Gb; marginal dies pass without row sparing.

title: Bit-granular weak-cell extraction into an on-die patch SRAM
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: at wafer sort the 0.01-0.1% of cells with retention under 1 s are pulled out individually; a small per-bank address CAM plus SRAM data bits shadows them, so array refresh is set by the median cell (seconds) instead of the 13 fA tail.
why: Refresh interval 64 ms to ~1 s (16x fewer refreshes, ~15-30% idle power saved) for ~0.3% die area; Cs could drop ~20% because the tail no longer sets the spec.

title: Mat-location-tuned ECC strength map from fail-bit statistics
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: mats at array edges, next to sense-amp stripes or on known litho hotspots borrow spare columns to run a t=2-3 BCH code while interior mats keep SEC; the strength map is fused at sort from fail-bit-map statistics.
why: Spends parity only where errors cluster: ~30-40% less total parity at equal FIT, or 10x higher raw BER tolerated in hotspot mats, raising yield of aggressive cells.

title: Z-channel asymmetric code with minority-charge data inversion
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: retention failures are almost only charged-to-discharged, so each word stores an inversion flag that minimizes charged cells (using the known true/anti-cell polarity of each row) and is protected by a Z-channel asymmetric code that corrects only charge-loss flips.
why: Asymmetric codes need ~30-40% fewer check bits for equal correction, and at most half the cells are ever charged, halving leakage exposure; relaxes the retention-tail spec ~2-4x.

title: Refresh doubles as scrub via per-subarray syndrome engines
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a small shared syndrome/correct engine on each subarray sense-amp stripe checks every row while it sits in the sense amps during its refresh activation and writes corrected bits back before precharge.
why: Every row is scrubbed every refresh window (vs DDR5 ECS ~once per 24 h, >1000x more often), so single-bit errors never accumulate into uncorrectable doubles; tolerates ~100x weaker cells for ~2-3% area.

title: Unused repair spares reborn as hammer-shadow and parity rows
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the 30-60% of redundant rows/columns left unused after repair get a second job; an on-die table exposes them so the controller migrates hammered hot rows into them and stores extra parity there for a stronger code.
why: Reclaims ~2-4% of die area already paid for as a live reliability resource; raises the effective hammer threshold and correction strength at zero extra silicon.

title: Three nested codes sized to relax cell BER to 1e-6
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting (Matryoshka): inner on-die SEC per 128 bits fixes scattered bits, a middle cross-device symbol code per cache line fixes dead mats/chips, and an outer controller-side XOR erasure code across each 4 KB page group (invoked only on rare uncorrectables) rebuilds whole lines; budgets are co-designed so raw cell BER can be 1e-6 instead of ~1e-12.
why: A ~10^6x relaxed raw error target permits ~25-35% smaller Cs (attacks the 4.5-5.4 fF charge wall) or 4-8x longer refresh at ~15% total parity.

title: Negative counter-pulse on neighbor wordlines cancels hammer electrons
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: after each aggressor precharge, the two adjacent wordlines are driven ~0.3 V more negative for ~2 ns, creating a counter-field that sweeps electrons injected from the aggressor channel back before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Fact 9 row hammer (~1k activations): if migrating charge dominates, the flip threshold could rise 5-10x with no counters, costing only a local pump and driver timing.

title: Per-boot keyed Feistel scramble of physical row adjacency
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: an on-die 4-round Feistel network keyed by a per-boot random seed permutes logical-to-physical rows within each subarray and is re-keyed incrementally each refresh window, so an attacker cannot know which logical rows sandwich a victim.
why: Double- and many-sided hammer patterns become blind guesses; attack cost rises by about the subarray size (~512x), relaxing the hammer threshold needed for cheaper, denser cells.

title: Factory weak-cell dictionary turns errors into cheap erasures
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: each die's weak-cell addresses found at sort are compressed into on-package antifuse/NOR storage and loaded into the decoder at boot, which treats those positions as erasures (one check symbol each instead of two for an unknown error).
why: About 2x correction capability from the same parity, so dies failing today's retention bins pass; a few % yield plus longer refresh at no area cost.

title: Rewritable on-die remap CAM for lifetime self-retirement
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: replace one-shot antifuse post-package repair with an SRAM remap CAM loaded from a small rewritable on-die store and backed by a 1-2% hidden row reserve, so the scrubber retires rows as they begin failing, SSD bad-block style, an unlimited number of times.
why: Cells ship with less aging margin because degradation is absorbed in the field; ~10-20% retention guardband reclaimed as smaller Cs or longer refresh.

title: Constant-bias shield line between adjacent buried wordlines
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: a narrow buried line held at a fixed negative potential sits between neighboring wordlines where the passing gate used to face the storage node, so the victim never sees the aggressor's 3 V swing or its trap-mediated electron flow.
why: Targets the passing-gate path behind the ~1k hammer threshold, aiming at 10x higher thresholds and lower GIDL for ~6F2 to 6.5F2 area.

title: Sense-amp resolution time as soft-decision reliability information
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way around: instead of waiting for bits to fail, each sense amp's latch time is compared with a delayed strobe; slow-resolving (low-margin) bits are flagged as soft erasures to the ECC decoder and queued for migration.
why: Soft-decision decoding gives ~2x correction or ~10x lower uncorrectable rate from the same parity and finds weak cells before they flip, letting refresh stretch ~2x.

title: Rounded trench and junction corners to clip GIDL tail
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality/curvature: a hydrogen anneal reflows silicon so buried-wordline trench bottoms and storage-node contact edges reach radii of 3 nm or more, lowering the peak junction field that drives trap-assisted tunnelling in the worst cells.
why: Fact 3: 20-30% lower peak field can cut tail leakage ~5-10x (exponential in field), stretching refresh ~4x.

title: ECC-tracked adaptive negative wordline off-level per bank
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: the fixed wordline-off voltage becomes a per-bank 4-bit DAC; when on-die ECC sees correctable retention errors rise (hot, aged or weak bank) it drives VNWL deeper (-0.2 to -0.5 V) to cut subthreshold leakage, then relaxes it to save pump energy and GIDL.
why: Leakage-tail suppression on demand: ~2-4x retention in the worst banks without a global worst-case setting; ~30% less refresh energy.

title: Bit-significance placement: exponent in strong rows, mantissa in leaky
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: the controller splits BF16/FP8 tensors so sign/exponent bits go to fully refreshed, ECC-protected rows while low mantissa bits go to rows refreshed 16x less often or to weak-binned dies, sold as an AI-grade memory SKU.
why: ~50% of AI-resident bits escape the refresh and tail spec: ~40% less refresh energy, and weak dies otherwise scrapped become sellable capacity.

title: Vertical XOR parity tier rescues defective layers in 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: in a monolithic 3D DRAM with N tiers, one tier per vertical string stores XOR parity of the bits above it, so a whole failed tier, string segment or leaky-tier tail can be rebuilt by reading the column.
why: Fact 2: tier yield compounds (0.98^26 = 59%); tolerating one bad tier per string lifts yield to ~90% and makes 26+ tier break-even reachable with weaker lateral transistors.

title: Spectral Goertzel detector spots periodic hammer patterns cheaply
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration/resonance: per-bank Goertzel filters run on hashed activation-address streams; a hammer loop shows up as a sharp spectral line at the attacker's loop frequency and triggers targeted neighbor refresh for the hashed rows.
why: Detects hammering with a few thousand gates instead of KB-scale per-row counter tables (~10x less area than per-row-counter tracking); a tiny counter covers aperiodic attacks.

title: Periodic in-situ microheater anneal heals VRT traps
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: TiN heater strips beside each mat run a few-millisecond 300-400 C local anneal during maintenance windows, with data evacuated to neighbor mats, detrapping the oxide/interface defects behind variable retention time and hammer susceptibility.
why: Resets aging and VRT tails in the field, potentially restoring 2-5x retention in degraded mats and letting cells ship with less end-of-life guardband.

title: Continuous stressed-read margin probing predicts failing cells
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: idle bank cycles run nonstop stressed reads with a shortened sensing delay and an offset reference, the DRAM analog of flash read-retry, so cells drifting toward failure are found and migrated weeks before they flip.
why: Turns idle time into predictive reliability: ~10x fewer uncorrectable events and less shipped margin, needing only a reference trim beyond existing circuits.

title: Close wordline early, keep row buffer latched to cap RowPress
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping/rushing: wordline-on time is decoupled from row-open time; the wordline drops as soon as restore completes while the isolated sense amps keep serving reads as a row buffer, and writes trigger a brief re-raise.
why: Aggressor-on time (RowPress) is capped near minimum tRAS regardless of open-page policy, cutting press-induced flips ~10-100x while keeping open-page hit performance.

title: Unrepaired weak cells kept as live refresh-rate governors
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: instead of repairing every weak cell, ~1,000 known-weak cells per bank stay in place holding a known pattern; checking them each window measures real leakage (temperature, aging, radiation) and sets refresh just above their failure point.
why: Replaces worst-case 64/32 ms guardbands with measured margin: ~2-4x fewer refreshes at typical temperatures, and repair resources are saved for clusters.

title: ECC-cluster feedback trims individual sense-amp offsets
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: when correctable errors cluster on one bitline, the controller writes a per-sense-amp offset trim (small capacitor or back-bias DAC loaded from a trim RAM), fixing the weak-sense-amp part of the tail instead of sparing the column.
why: Much of the effective retention tail is SA offset, not cell leakage; trimming lets ~10-20% smaller signal (smaller Cs) be sensed reliably and saves spare columns.

title: U.S. reliability-broker buffer remediates sub-spec domestic DRAM dies
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: a CXL/DIMM buffer chip fabbed on a U.S. mature logic line (12-22 nm class in New York) runs a strong LDPC code plus row remap over dies from U.S. DRAM fabs that fail JEDEC retention or hammer bins, and the module ships as spec-compliant.
why: Turns 5-15% of domestic wafer output now scrapped or downbinned into sellable capacity through an all-U.S. chain; ~10% lower cost per usable bit.

title: Small-die tile DRAM on depreciated U.S. lines plus erasure coding
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation under the U.S.-only rule: dies are split into 1-2 Gb tiles made on fully depreciated, EUV-free domestic DRAM nodes, and many tiles are packaged at a U.S. OSAT with a U.S. logic die that rides through a dead tile with tile-level erasure coding.
why: Small dies yield higher and depreciated tools cut wafer cost ~40-50% (depreciation is ~55% of cost), so domestic bits get cheaper without new EUV fabs.

title: Domestic molybdenum dual-work-function buried wordline replaces tungsten
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: tungsten (China ~80%) is replaced by molybdenum from U.S. mines in the buried wordline; Mo needs no thick TiN barrier, which frees room for a low-work-function lower segment next to the storage-node junction that softens the gate-to-drain field.
why: Removes the tungsten chokepoint, cuts GIDL in tail cells ~3-5x and lowers wordline resistance ~20-30% in narrow trenches: a refresh and supply-security win.

title: Asymmetric storage-node-side implant using U.S.-built ion implanters
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: a tilted, shadowed implant on domestically built implanters grades only the storage-node side of the access transistor with a light, deep LDD and no halo, while the bitline side keeps strong doping for drive current.
why: Lowers junction field and trap-assisted tunnelling at the storage node, the leakage-tail source, ~3-10x while keeping write speed, with all-domestic tooling.

title: VRT provocation pulses expose flickering cells in minutes
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: during wafer test on U.S.-made memory ATE, short high-field gate/junction toggle pulses force variable-retention-time traps to switch states repeatedly, so VRT cells reveal themselves in minutes instead of multi-day retention soaks and are mapped out.
why: VRT is why refresh guardbands cannot be cut; reliable screening could allow 2-4x longer refresh and shortens test time, a key cost of a U.S. backend.

title: N+1 hot-spare die in U.S.-assembled memory stacks
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: every domestically assembled 8-high stack carries a ninth die; base-die BIST tracks per-die error rates and, when one degrades, migrates its contents in the background and switches its channel to the spare.
why: Stack yield and field life no longer hinge on the worst of 8 dies; recovers part of the 20-30% stacking yield loss (fact 6) and permits more aggressive cell designs.

title: Federal procurement buys system-level reliability, not component spec
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way around: U.S. government and CHIPS-funded buyers specify DRAM by delivered system FIT (component plus certified ECC/remap firmware) instead of JEDEC raw cell margins, creating a guaranteed market for U.S.-made sub-spec dies remediated in U.S. modules.
why: Lets domestic fabs ship 5-15% more bits per wafer and underwrites U.S. capacity, aimed at U.S. manufacturability and cost per bit.

title: Microfluidic channels etched in U.S.-made stack base die
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics/hydraulics: coolant microchannels are etched into the domestically fabbed logic base die and capped with a bonded silicon lid, so liquid flows directly under the stack and holds DRAM dies at 60 C or below instead of 85-95 C.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C drop, so ~4x longer refresh and no hot 2x-refresh mode; retention-weak dies pass, raising U.S. stack yield.

title: Molybdenum-filled TSVs match silicon expansion, shrinking stress zones
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: through-silicon vias are filled with domestic molybdenum (CTE ~5 ppm/K, near silicon's ~3) instead of copper (~17), removing the thermomechanical stress that degrades retention of nearby cells and forces keep-out zones.
why: Shrinks keep-out area and stress-related retention tails near TSVs, reclaiming part of the HBM area tax (fact 6) with no imported fill metal; Mo's higher resistivity is tolerable over 30-50 um vias.

title: Air gaps between buried wordlines cut hammer coupling
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: a sacrificial carbon spacer between neighboring buried wordlines is ashed out through a pinch-off cap using U.S.-vendor deposition/etch tools, leaving an air gap (k=1) that weakens capacitive and field coupling from aggressor to victim.
why: Coupling capacitance drops ~40-50%; if hammer flips track coupling the threshold rises severalfold and wordline RC falls too, with domestic tools and chemicals.

title: ALD alumina hydrogen-lock cap preserves interface passivation
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells/thin films: a thin ALD Al2O3 shell is deposited over the array right after the forming-gas anneal with domestic ALD tools and precursors, so hydrogen passivating gate-oxide and STI interface traps cannot outgas during later BEOL thermal steps.
why: Fewer active interface traps means a thinner trap-assisted leakage tail and fewer VRT cells, targeting ~2x longer refresh with no new tool class or imported material.

title: Ozone radical healing of oxygen vacancies in capacitor dielectric
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: after the ZrO2-based capacitor stack is deposited (zirconium from U.S. refiners), a low-temperature ozone/oxygen-radical anneal fills oxygen vacancies that form leakage paths through the thin dielectric in the worst pillars.
why: Cuts the capacitor contribution to the leakage tail and allows ~10% thinner dielectric (more Cs per pillar), attacking fact 1 with domestic chemistry.

title: Borrow image-sensor dark-current tricks: pinned STI sidewall implant
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: DRAM retention leakage and CMOS-image-sensor dark current are the same generation physics, so copy the sensor playbook: a p+ pinning implant along the STI sidewall keeps storage-node depletion off interface traps, plus a carbon-co-implanted gettering layer in domestically grown epi wafers.
why: Image sensors cut dark current 10-100x this way; even 3-5x lower tail leakage stretches refresh ~4x using U.S. wafer and process capability.

title: Disposable two-year DRAM tier for checkpointed AI clusters
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: a U.S.-made memory SKU designed for 2-year service in AI training racks with frequent checkpoints skips long burn-in and 10-year aging guardbands, ships with in-field error telemetry, and is swapped and recycled like a consumable.
why: Less screening and guardband adds 5-10% sellable bits per wafer and cuts test cost, aimed at domestic cost per bit and capacity.

title: Maskless per-die repair wiring via domestic multi-beam e-beam
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics under the U.S.-only rule: after an early electrical test at first metal, a U.S.-built multi-column e-beam writer patterns a unique repair-routing layer per die that wires spare rows/columns in place of defective ones, with no fuses, lasers or masks.
why: Repair becomes layout instead of fuse banks (shrinking repair periphery, fact 7) and needs no foreign laser or scanner; yield rises because wiring defects fuses cannot fix become repairable.

title: Interference-litho array gratings with 6% spare bitlines
idea: TRIZ separation in space: the perfectly periodic array layers are patterned by mask-free laser interference lithography plus self-aligned multiple patterning on U.S.-built deposition/etch tools, leaving only relaxed-rule periphery for precision writing; stitch and standing-wave defects are absorbed by 6% spare bitlines and an ECC that knows defects arrive as whole columns.
why: Removes foreign scanners from array layers (5-7 EUV layers, fact 4) and cuts array patterning capital ~50%; reliability is bought with redundancy instead of tool perfection.

title: Errors as cache misses: detect-only DRAM refetches peer replica
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: for read-only AI weights replicated across a cluster, U.S.-made inference memory carries only a cheap CRC per 4 KB page; a detected error discards the page and refetches it from a peer node's copy over the fabric, so cells may run at raw BER ~1e-5.
why: Drops on-die ECC and most guardbands for this tier: ~6% parity reclaimed, refresh stretched ~10x and weak dies usable, at negligible refetch traffic.

title: Paraffin phase-change lid keeps stacks under 85 C
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: a sealed U.S.-made paraffin/fatty-acid phase-change pack bonded to the memory-stack lid melts at ~70 C, absorbing AI burst heat so DRAM never enters the 85 C+ double-refresh range, and refreezes between bursts.
why: Avoids the 2x refresh rate and retention-fail spikes during bursts (~10-15% bandwidth recovered at peak) and lets retention-marginal dies pass, using domestic petrochemical material.

title: National DRAM failure-telemetry exchange feeds back to U.S. fabs
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback at national scale: a CHIPS-funded, privacy-scrubbed exchange pools corrected-error, hammer and retention telemetry from U.S. hyperscalers per die lot, returning per-lot refresh/hammer settings to deployed systems and process-shift alerts to U.S. fabs.
why: Closes the field-to-fab loop: ~2x per-lot refresh relaxation and faster yield learning for domestic DRAM ramps (months saved against fact-4 capital timelines).

title: HZO nonvolatile shadow layer makes leaked cells recoverable
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: a thin ferroelectric HfZrO sublayer (hafnium and zirconium from U.S. refiners) sits in series with the linear capacitor dielectric; before long idle periods data is copied into polarization and refresh stops, and on wake a polarization read restores the charge.
why: Refresh vanishes for idle regions (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) and retention-tail losses become recoverable; limited ferroelectric endurance is spent only on idle/wake transitions.

title: Variable-pitch hammer-hardened row zone for page tables and kernels
idea: TRIZ separation by condition: each bank has a ~3% zone laid out at wider wordline pitch with larger capacitors on the same U.S. process; the OS places page tables, kernel and security metadata there while the dense 6F2 zone holds ordinary data with lighter mitigation.
why: Hammer attacks that matter (privilege escalation) hit the hardened zone, so the dense zone can accept lower thresholds and simpler trackers; suits a trusted domestic defense supply.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM that routes around dead tiles on-wafer
idea: TRIZ separation by scale: a whole 300 mm wafer is left undiced at a U.S. fab; 1,000+ DRAM tiles join through a stitched on-wafer mesh and at power-on a route table skips dead tiles and reticle-stitch faults, yielding one ~1-2 TB memory slab with no packaging, TSVs or foreign OSAT.
why: Defects become routing problems instead of scrapped dies: nearly all good tiles used, packaging and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) avoided, fully domestic.

title: Probe-free wafer-level retention soaks via on-die BIST
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution: tester-bound retention testing is replaced by on-die BIST that runs multi-hour, multi-temperature retention and hammer profiling while whole wafers sit in U.S.-built burn-in ovens on a power-only contact; results are read out later in one quick touchdown.
why: Long tail screening becomes cheap (cost scales with oven space, not ATE time), so retention bins get fine-grained and good dies run longer refresh; less dependence on tester capacity.
